```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
library(Cohort2Trajectory)
```

## Before generation

Complete the [configuration](a01_configuration.html) and
[data import](a02_import.html) before calling `createTrajectories()`. Use the same
`studyEnv` throughout. The target cohort defines observation bounds; the state
cohorts define clinical intervals. Generation applies the selection, transition
and absorbing-state rules to those intervals.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
getDataForStudy(cdm = cdm, studyEnv = studyEnv)
trajectories <- createTrajectories(cdm = cdm, studyEnv = studyEnv)
```

For local data, omit `cdm` and configure `useCDM = FALSE`. Generation requires a
successful import; a failed import must be rerun before generation can proceed.

## Discrete trajectories

Discrete trajectories assign one state to each cycle. `cycleLength` is the
number of calendar days per cycle; use seven for weekly trajectories:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
trajectories <- createTrajectories(
  cdm = cdm,
  studyEnv = studyEnv,
  trajectoryType = "Discrete",
  stateSelectionType = "Priority",
  cycleLength = 7
)
```

Cycles begin at the target start date and include both endpoint dates. The last
cycle is shortened at the observation boundary. This example uses the priority
order configured in `studyEnv`.

The three selection methods choose among states that overlap the cycle and are
allowed by the transition rules:

| Method | Selection within a cycle |
| --- | --- |
| `"First"` | Choose the interval with the earliest start date, including intervals that began before the cycle. Resolve equal start dates using the priority order. |
| `"Overlap"` | Choose the state covering the most distinct days in the cycle. Combine separate intervals for the same state without counting overlapping days twice. Resolve equal coverage using the priority order. |
| `"Priority"` | Choose the highest-ranked state present during any part of the cycle. |

All three methods require every clinical state in `stateCohortPriorityOrder`,
highest priority first.

With `mergeStates = TRUE`, selection uses the combined states created during
import and their resolved rules. See [Configuration](a01_configuration.html) for
membership, inheritance and `mergedState()` overrides. Omitting an override's
`allowedTransitions` inherits destinations; supplying `NULL`, `character(0)` or
`list()` permits none. Absorbing status is a separate property.

Option names are case-insensitive and ignore surrounding spaces. Use names,
rather than numeric choice codes.

## Continuous trajectories

Continuous trajectories use calendar intervals. They do not use `cycleLength`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
trajectories <- createTrajectories(
  cdm = cdm,
  studyEnv = studyEnv,
  trajectoryType = "Continuous",
  stateSelectionType = "Priority"
)
```

In continuous mode, `"First"` and `"Overlap"` both retain bounded input intervals
that pass the transition rules, including overlaps.

`"Priority"` assigns shared days to the highest-priority permitted state. It can
shorten or split lower-priority intervals and requires every clinical state in
the priority order. Continuing an uninterrupted interval does not require a
self-transition when an unrelated record starts or ends.

Gaps remain unfilled. Simultaneous records retain their dates and equal elapsed
times, so row order does not establish within-day event order. Models requiring
distinct event times need a tie-handling rule.

## Transition rules and gaps

An empty `allowedStatesList` allows unrestricted transitions. Otherwise, each
transition source needs one named entry containing its allowed destinations.
Use `character(0)` for a source with none. Source names must match state labels
exactly; destination matching is case-insensitive. Merged studies require an
entry for every original state, including absorbing states. The first clinical
state and the `START` and `EXIT` markers need no incoming rule.

For nonmerged studies, destinations must be configured states, observed states
or a named discrete gap fallback. Configured states remain valid when absent
from the data. Unknown destinations are rejected before trajectory or settings
files are replaced.

Rules use each patient's last retained clinical state. Rejected records do not
change that source. Only permitted states compete for a discrete cycle; in
continuous mode, prohibited records are removed before the absorbing cutoff.

When no state can be selected for a discrete cycle, `oocFix` controls the result:

- `"None"` or `"OUT OF COHORT"` leaves the cycle as `OUT OF COHORT`.
- `"Last present state"` carries the last selected state forward only when its
  self-transition is allowed. Before the first selected state, the gap remains
  `OUT OF COHORT`.
- A state label supplies a named fallback, provided the transition to it is
  allowed. Use its exact spelling. For merged states, use the display label, not
  the internal `state_key`.

`OUT OF COHORT` is an unresolved cycle within observation. It does not reset the
last selected state for later transition checks. `"None"` and
`"Last present state"` always select gap behavior, even if a clinical label has that spelling.
These rules apply only to discrete output.

## Observation boundaries and absorbing states

By default, the first target interval supplies each patient's start and end
dates. With `targetEpisodeHandling = "All"`, each target period supplies its own
bounds. Periods without clinical state records remain eligible unless mandatory
rules exclude them. Their discrete cycles follow the gap rule; continuous output
contains only boundary markers.

State intervals are bounded by the target interval unless
`outOfCohortAllowed = TRUE`. This lets retained records extend its end, but not
its start. Set it during import to keep later records: generation cannot recover
discarded records. Local input needs a target row for every included patient.

Only a selected, permitted absorbing state ends follow-up early within a period.
No further transitions are checked in that period after it.

Discrete output stops after the absorbing cycle, using the cycle's dates.
Absorption does not shorten that cycle to the original event date; an observation
boundary on that date does. Continuous follow-up ends at the retained absorbing
interval's end date, and earlier overlapping intervals are capped there.

`START` marks the trajectory start. `EXIT` marks the day after the final cycle or
continuous follow-up endpoint. Neither marker adds observed time or indicates
death by itself.

## Multiple observation periods

The default, `targetEpisodeHandling = "First"`, uses one target interval per
patient. Use `"All"` to generate a separate episode for every distinct target
interval. Each episode has its own `START` and `EXIT`, cycles, elapsed time and
sequence counts. Transitions and carry-forward also restart; gaps between target
periods produce no rows. State IDs and any merged-state dictionary remain
study-wide, and `batchSize` still counts patients.

Here one patient has two periods separated by a gap. `Discharged` is absorbing
within the first period. The later admission is retained because
`stopAfterAbsorbingEpisode` defaults to `FALSE`. Use `TRUE` for a terminal outcome,
such as death, that should exclude subsequent observation periods.

```{r multiple-periods, results='hide', message=FALSE}
periods <- data.frame(
  subject_id = "001",
  cohort_definition_id = c("0", "0", "In hospital", "Discharged", "In hospital"),
  cohort_start_date = as.Date("2020-01-01") + c(0, 21, 0, 3, 21),
  cohort_end_date = as.Date("2020-01-01") + c(6, 27, 2, 3, 27)
)
episodePath <- tempfile("c2t-episodes-")
dir.create(episodePath)
episodeStudy <- cohort2TrajectoryConfiguration(
  studyName = "episodes",
  pathToStudy = episodePath,
  useCDM = FALSE,
  trajectoryDataObject = periods,
  stateCohortLabels = c("In hospital", "Discharged"),
  stateCohortPriorityOrder = c("Discharged", "In hospital"),
  stateCohortAbsorbing = "Discharged",
  stateSelectionType = "Priority",
  trajectoryType = "Discrete",
  cycleLength = 7,
  targetEpisodeHandling = "All"
)
getDataForStudy(studyEnv = episodeStudy)
episodeTrajectories <- createTrajectories(studyEnv = episodeStudy)
```

```{r multiple-periods-output}
knitr::kable(episodeTrajectories[c(
  "subject_id", "episode_id", "state_label", "state_start_date", "state_end_date"
)], row.names = FALSE)
```

For a fresh study, change suppression at generation:

```{r multiple-periods-stop, results='hide', message=FALSE}
firstEpisodeOnly <- createTrajectories(
  studyEnv = episodeStudy,
  stopAfterAbsorbingEpisode = TRUE
)
```

```{r multiple-periods-checks, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  identical(unique(episodeTrajectories$episode_id), 1:2),
  identical(unique(firstEpisodeOnly$episode_id), 1L)
)
```

Only a selected, permitted absorbing state triggers suppression. A rejected
absorbing record does not suppress later episodes. With suppression disabled,
later episodes start independently of an earlier absorbing outcome.

Input periods must not overlap; adjacent periods are allowed and identical
duplicates are removed. State records spanning several periods are clipped to
each. Mandatory-state requirements apply per episode; IDs are assigned before
that filtering and can therefore have gaps. `outOfCohortAllowed = TRUE` is
incompatible with `"All"`. Changing the period policy requires reimport.

The current TMA reader rejects this multi-episode format. See
[Read the output](a05_output.html#handing-the-result-to-an-analysis-package)
before using it in downstream analysis.

## Clinical history and event timing

Define history in the state cohorts. Separate death states with and without
prior pneumonia can preserve that distinction, but the package does not derive
it from labels. If pneumonia and death fall in one weekly cycle, selection may
retain only the death label. Its cycle dates cannot establish onset, elapsed
time between events or same-day ordering. Use continuous output or cleaned
intervals when the analysis needs those dates; see [Read the output](a05_output.html).

To model onset before mortality, generate aligned weekly views: one retaining
pneumonia history in the terminal week, and one where death takes priority.
Use identical patient-week boundaries and endpoints. TMA's
`prepareStageObservations()` pairs the views within each week before
`estimateStageTransitions()` estimates the stages, rather than treating them
as independent weekly sequences. See TMA's `inst/examples/c2t-to-icer.R`.

## Saved studies and output

Fresh studies accept generation overrides as above. To change mandatory-state
requirements, rerun `getDataForStudy()` first: these determine which patients
are imported.

A completed fresh run saves its rules in `Settings/analysisSettings.rds`.
CDM settings also contain the imported cohort definitions; patient records are
stored separately. See [Import cohort data](a02_import.html) for saved-study
setup and settings compatibility.

After configuring a study with `runSavedStudy = TRUE`, import fresh data and use
the restored analysis settings without overrides:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
getDataForStudy(cdm = newCdm, studyEnv = studyEnv)
trajectories <- createTrajectories(cdm = newCdm, studyEnv = studyEnv)
```

Saved CDM runs use the embedded cohort definitions. Saved local runs need fresh
local input. Configure a new study to change the saved analysis rules.

`createTrajectories()` returns a data frame and saves a CSV in `Data` after all
patient batches finish. A batch error does not replace it with a partial result.

With `useCDM = TRUE` and a supplied CDM object, generation joins age and gender,
including after a local import. Otherwise, `age` and `gender_concept_id` are
`NA`. See [Read the output](a05_output.html) for the schema and saved files.
